finalAnswer: The remaining word after all leftmost pattern deletions.
shortExplanation: Build a clean output prefix one character at a time. Whenever its final characters equal the forbidden pattern, remove that suffix.
detailedSteps: Keep the unread characters in their original order and an output prefix containing no occurrence of the pattern.
Append the next character. An occurrence introduced by this append must end at that character, so compare only the final $m$ positions.
If the suffix matches, remove it. This is the leftmost occurrence in the current full word: an earlier start would have an earlier end and would already have appeared in the clean prefix.
After the deletion, the output is a prefix of the previously clean output. It is clean again, so one suffix removal suffices for this appended character.
Every deletion therefore follows the required order. When all characters are read, the clean output is exactly the final censored word.
Each append compares at most $m$ characters. Time is $O(Nm)$, at most $10^8$ character-comparison opportunities under the original bounds; memory is $O(N+m)$.
keyIdeas: A clean prefix makes any newly found match a suffix.
Equal-length occurrences are ordered by their ending positions as well as their starting positions.
commonMistakes: Removing a later occurrence can change the result; always preserve the leftmost deletion order.
A removal can expose a new match at the join, so checking only occurrences in the original word misses cases.
Repeatedly shifting the entire million-character word can be too slow.
difficultyNotes: The main issue is preserving the repeated leftmost rule, including matches exposed by deletions. With a pattern of at most 100 characters, direct suffix comparison fits the source bounds.

shortExplanation: Scan left to right and count partial subsequences. A C starts a new partial word, an O extends every earlier C, and a W completes every earlier CO.
detailedSteps: Maintain three 64-bit counts: $c$ for earlier C letters, $co$ for earlier CO subsequences, and $cow$ for complete COW subsequences.
For a C, increase $c$ by one. For an O, add $c$ to $co$. For a W, add $co$ to $cow$.
Every newly counted subsequence ends at the character just read. Its earlier indices were already counted, so their order is correct and each indexed sequence is counted exactly once.
Different subsequences may share positions, as allowed. The three mutually exclusive character branches do not reuse the same position twice inside one subsequence.
At the end, return $cow$. The scan takes $O(N)$ time and uses $O(1)$ counters beyond the input word.
Use 64-bit integers for every count. There are at most $\binom{N}{3}$ indexed triples, and at $N=100000$ this is $166661666700000$; even an intermediate CO count can exceed 32 bits.
keyIdeas: Extend already counted partial subsequences when their next letter arrives.
Counting indexed choices naturally permits different occurrences to share letters.
commonMistakes: Searching only for contiguous COW strings ignores allowed skipped letters.
Using a 32-bit pair counter can overflow before the final triple count is computed.
Updating partial counts in an order that lets one character fill two positions breaks the index ordering.
difficultyNotes: The prefix-count invariant is short, but all intermediate counts need 64-bit arithmetic, not only the printed answer.

finalAnswer: Number of valid paths through the colored grid.
shortExplanation: Count paths ending at each cell. Sum the counts from earlier rows and earlier columns whose cells have the opposite color.
detailedSteps: Let $f[r][c]$ count paths ending at cell $(r,c)$. Set $f[0][0]=1$ for the starting path prefix.
For every other cell, inspect all predecessors $(i,j)$ with $i<r$, $j<c$, and a different color. Add $f[i][j]$ for each of them.
The last jump of every valid path has one unique predecessor. The sum includes precisely the allowed jumps, so it counts every complete path once.
Evaluate cells in row-major order. Every valid predecessor is in an earlier row, so its count is ready. Other cells in the first row or first column stay zero.
The answer is $f[R-1][C-1]$. Time is $O(R^2C^2)$ and space is $O(RC)$; the maximum grid has only 11025 predecessor pairs to inspect.
No modulus is specified. Ignoring colors gives at most $\binom{R+C-4}{R-2}\le\binom{26}{13}=10400600$ paths, so all sums are exact with the integer type used here.
keyIdeas: Strictly increasing rows make the grid dependencies acyclic.
Split paths by their unique final predecessor.
commonMistakes: Both coordinates must increase strictly; a jump in the same row or column is invalid.
Forward movement does not make a same-color jump valid.
Leaving the start count at zero makes every later count zero.
difficultyNotes: The direct path recurrence is enough for a 15 by 15 grid. The important details are the two strict inequalities, the color change, and the initial start count.
